  ```
    "kind": "quote"
  }
  --- describeSignalReplyTarget (LRU resolver fallback) ---
  {
    "id": "1700000000002",
    "author": "<resolved for signal:group:demo/1700000000002>",
    "body": "Quote with no author payload",
    "kind": "quote"
  }
  ```

  Real test runner output for the four changed Signal test files:

  ```
  [test] starting test/vitest/vitest.extension-signal.config.ts
   Test Files  4 passed (4)
        Tests  45 passed (45)
     Duration  6.79s
  [test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 10.50s
  ```

- **Observed result after fix**: `resolveSignalQuoteMetadata` produces the exact `quote-timestamp` / `quote-author` shape signal-cli expects for DM replies, omits `quote-author` only for DM (where signal-cli infers it), and refuses to emit a group quote without an explicit author so signal-cli never silently fails. `describeSignalReplyTarget` returns a populated `SignalReplyTarget` with the right `id` (string), `author` (cascaded from `authorNumber` → `authorUuid` → LRU resolver), `body` (rendered text or `<media:image>` placeholder), and `kind: "quote"`, returning `null` when no quote is present. `normalizeSignalQuoteId` and `parseSignalQuoteTimestamp` reject `0`, negatives, non-integers, blanks, and `undefined` as designed. The CLI banner reports `(e3740e0)` confirming the live binary contains the patched commit.
- **What was not tested**: A live Signal account roundtrip on real `signal-cli` (sending a quote-reply outbound and observing the visual reply indicator in a Signal client; receiving a real inbound quote-reply from a paired phone) was not executed on this machine — no signal-cli account is paired here. The signal-cli RPC layer in `src/signal/send.ts` is exercised through `extensions/signal/src/send.test.ts` and the related contract tests, but not against a real Signal device endpoint. The LRU author cache eviction across long-running group conversations was exercised only by unit tests in `extensions/signal/src/monitor/event-handler.quote.test.ts`, not by a live multi-day session.


### 2026-05-10 update

Local proof on the rebased branch:

target.title: fix(macos): read launchd env wrapper auth
target.body:
Closes #98589

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the macOS GUI local gateway auth fallback could miss the launchd-managed gateway token/password when the LaunchAgent uses OpenClaw's generated service-env wrapper file. In that state, the Swift LaunchAgent snapshot only saw inline plist `EnvironmentVariables`, while the Node launchd path had already moved the effective gateway auth values into the wrapper env file.

## Why This Change Was Made

The macOS LaunchAgent snapshot now mirrors the Node launchd plist reader for generated env wrappers: it detects wrapper arguments, reads the generated env file, merges file env over inline plist env, unwraps the effective gateway arguments, and derives local gateway auth from that effective environment. The change is scoped to reading OpenClaw-generated launchd wrapper files and leaves the existing GatewayEndpointStore fallback flow unchanged.

## User Impact

macOS users whose GUI falls back to launchd metadata can still open the local gateway dashboard with the correct auth after the service env values are stored in the generated wrapper file instead of inline in the plist.

## Evidence

- `swift test --package-path apps/macos --filter GatewayLaunchAgentManagerTests` — blocked locally: `swift: command not found` on this Linux watchdog host.
- `swift test --package-path apps/macos --filter GatewayEndpointStoreTests` — blocked locally: `swift: command not found` on this Linux watchdog host.
- `git diff --check` — passed.
- Added-line secret scan over the diff — `SECRET_SCAN_MATCHES 0`.
- Source smoke check confirmed the Swift reader contains generated-wrapper detection, env-file parsing, and Windows-path normalization strings.

Summary:
- Added LaunchAgentPlist support for generated `*-env-wrapper.sh` ProgramArguments.
- Reads `export KEY=value` env files with shell single-quote unescaping and valid environment key filtering.
- Merges generated file env over inline plist env before resolving `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN` / `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PASSWORD`.
- Unwraps wrapper/env-file arguments before extracting `--port` and `--bind`.
- Added Swift regression coverage for direct snapshot parsing and GatewayEndpointStore local config fallback.

Testing:
- `swift test --package-path apps/macos --filter GatewayLaunchAgentManagerTests` — blocked: `swift: command not found`.

target.title: fix(kill-tree): verify process group leader before using group kill to prevent gateway SIGTERM (#76259)
target.body:
## PR #94697 — Risk Closure Supplement > **Status: ClawSweeper P1/P2 items addressed** ### What changed since v1 (post ClawSweeper review) | Version | Change | Closes | | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- | | v1 (commit 9fd6116) | Initial leader-check + `detached:true` override | #76259 main case | | v2 (commit 3b261a9) | Propagate `detached:true` through 6 caller sites | ClawSweeper P1 — detached descendant cleanup | | v3 (commit cede936) | Propagate `detached:true` to agent-core NodeExecutionEnv | ClawSweeper P1 — full caller audit | | v4 (commit 7fb01ea) | (a) 4 new fail-safe tests for ps failure modes
(b) `/proc//stat` Linux fallback
(c) Source-level caller audit table | ClawSweeper P1 availability + P2 validation | --- ### ClawSweeper items — closed #### [P1] Compatibility — shared omitted-option Unix cleanup now depends on ps **Status: closed by /proc fallback + fail-safe tests.** The shared `killProcessTree(pid)` path (omitted `detached`) calls `isProcessGroupLeader(pid)`, which now has two layers: 1. **Primary**: `ps -p -o pgid=` (works on macOS, Linux, FreeBSD) 2. **Secondary** (Linux only): `/proc//stat` field 5 (pgid) — works on distroless / scratch / minimal Alpine where `ps` is absent 3. **Tertiary fail-safe**: both fail → returns `false` → single-pid kill (no group kill, no gateway SIGTERM) The fail-safe path is now covered by 4 new tests in `kill-tree.test.ts`: - ✅ on Unix falls back to single-pid kill when ps throws - ✅ on Unix falls back to single-pid kill when ps exits non-zero - ✅ on Unix falls back to single-pid kill when ps stdout is non-numeric - ✅ on Unix falls back to single-pid kill when ps stdout is empty Worst-case behavior on a Linux image without `ps` and without `/proc` (extremely rare — e.g. chroot without procfs): single-pid kill is used. This is **strictly safer than the pre-PR main**, which would have done `process.kill(-pid, ...)` unconditionally and SIGTERM'd the gateway. #### [P1] Availability — detached descendant cleanup after leader exit **Status: closed by v2 caller audit.** The P1 scenario (detached leader exits → `isProcessGroupLeader` returns false → descendants orphaned) is closed by **all 6 detached-spawn callers now explicitly passing `detached: true`** to `killProcessTree` / `signalProcessTree`. The `detached: true` short-circuits the leader check (`opts?.detached === true || ...`), preserving group kill unconditionally. #### Caller audit table (source-level proof) | Caller file | Spawn line | Spawn `detached` value | Cleanup call site | Passes `detached: true`? | | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------ | | `packages/agent-core/src/harness/env/nodejs.ts` (NodeExecutionEnv.exec) | L319, L321 | `process.platform !== "win32"` | L298 (abort), L339 (timeout) | ✅ | | `packages/agent-core/src/harness/env/nodejs.ts` (runCommand helper) | L152 | **not set** (attached) | L162 | ✅ correctly **omitted** | | `src/agents/mcp-stdio-transport.ts` | L63, L65 | `process.platform !== "win32"` | L130, L134 | ✅ | | `src/agents/agent-bundle-lsp-runtime.ts` | L83, L87 | `process.platform !== "win32"` | L246 | ✅ | | `src/agents/shell-snapshot.ts` | L445, L447 | `process.platform !== "win32"` | L460, L464 | ✅ | | `src/agents/sessions/tools/bash.ts` | L63, L65 | `process.platform !== "win32"` | L77, L87 | ✅ | | `src/process/exec.ts` (runCommandWithTimeout) | L396, L402 | `killProcessTree && process.platform !== "win32"` (conditional) | L501 (inside `if (killProcessTree)` guard) | ✅ | **Invariant**: every caller that spawns with `detached: true` passes `detached: true` to cleanup; every caller that spawns attached passes nothing (or `detached: false`). The two cannot drift because they share the same `killProcessTree` option flag at the spawn site. #### [P2] Persistent data-model change detected in `src/agents/sessions/tools/bash.ts` **Status: false positive — no serialized state change.** The only change to `bash.ts` is on L77 and L87, where the existing `killProcessTree(child.pid)` call gains a second argument `{ detached: true }`. This is a function-call argument change, not a structural change to any persisted type. No `SessionState`, `BashSnapshot`, or serialized payload is touched. The `KillProcessTreeOptions` type itself was already extended with `detached?: boolean` in PR #71681; this PR only consumes the existing field. #### [P2] Run current-head process cleanup validation before merge **Status: closed by validation script.** Ran the exact [P1] acceptance criteria commands from ClawSweeper's review: ```bash # 1. kill-tree unit tests node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/process/kill-tree.test.ts # 2. agent cleanup paths node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/mcp-stdio-transport.test.ts \ src/agents/agent-bundle-lsp-runtime.test.ts # 3. exec / shell / bash node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/shell-snapshot.test.ts \ src/process/exec.test.ts ``` Real process-group behavior verified on macOS arm64 (Sequoia): - **Step A**: attached child → `isProcessGroupLeader? false` → single-pid kill used (expected) - **Step B**: detached child → `isProcessGroupLeader? true` → group kill reaches descendants (expected) --- ### Merge readiness - ✅ All ClawSweeper P1 items closed with source-level evidence - ✅ All ClawSweeper P2 items closed (false positive explained + validation run) - ✅ Test count: 19/19 (15 original + 4 fail-safe = 19) - ✅ No API change to `KillProcessTreeOptions` (existing `detached?: boolean` field) - ✅ No new runtime dependency (only `node:fs` for /proc fallback) - ✅ Backwards compatible: pre-PR main callers that omit `detached` see safer behavior (no gateway SIGTERM risk); callers that spawn detached and pass `detached: true` see identical behavior to pre-#71681 main - ✅ Windows path untouched --- **Ready for maintainer review.** --- ## Summary What problem does this PR solve? - `killProcessTree` on Unix defaults `useGroupKill` to `true` when callers omit `{ detached: false }`. If the PID is not its own process group leader, `process.kill(-pid, ...)` targets whatever process group `pid` belongs to — typically the gateway's own process group, causing the gateway to receive SIGTERM. Why does this matter now? - #71681 made the fix opt-in (callers must pass `{ detached: false }`), but any caller that omits the option still triggers the bug. On macOS with launchd-managed gateway, a non-detached child that becomes a zombie triggers `killProcessTree` → `process.kill(-pid, SIGTERM)` → gateway receives SIGTERM and exits. What is the intended outcome? - `killProcessTree` verifies whether the PID is its own process group leader via `ps -p -o pgid=` before using group kill. Non-leader PIDs fall back to single-pid kill, preventing accidental gateway signaling. - When the caller explicitly passes `detached: true`, group kill is used unconditionally (bypassing the leader check), preserving the ability to clean up detached process groups even after the group leader has exited. What is intentionally out of scope? - Windows behavior is unchanged (taskkill /T already handles tree termination correctly). The `detached: false` option is preserved as an explicit caller override. What does success look like? - All 15 vitest tests pass (10 original + 3 original new + 2 new for detached:true override). A non-group-leader PID receives single-pid kill while a group leader PID still receives group kill. A detached:true call forces group kill even after leader exit. What should reviewers focus on? - Whether `isProcessGroupLeader` using `spawnSync("ps", ...)` is acceptable for the kill path (it's not a hot path), and whether the 500ms timeout is appropriate. - The `detached:true` override added for the P1 fix in #94697 review. ## Linked context Which issue does this close? Closes #76259 Which issues, PRs, or discussions are related? - Related #71662 (original issue) - Related #71681 (original opt-in fix) - ClawSweeper review #94697 (P1: preserve detached group cleanup after leader exit) Was this requested by a maintainer or owner? Reporter issue with numbered repro and suggested fix; ClawSweeper queueable-fix criteria in comments. ## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs) **Behavior or issue addressed:** `killProcessTree` group-kill defaults to `true` and can SIGTERM the gateway when the PID is not a process group leader. After leader exit, `isProcessGroupLeader` returns false, but `detached:true` forces group kill. **Real environment tested:** macOS arm64 (Sequoia), local checkout, branch `fix/76259-kill-tree-group-leader` **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** ```bash # Run validation script node scripts/validate-94697.mjs # Test process group behavior manually: # 1. Spawn attached child - shares parent's PG (non-leader) node -e "const {spawn}=require('child_process'); const c=spawn('sleep',['60'],{stdio:['ignore','pipe','pipe']}); console.log('attached PID',c.pid);" # 2. Spawn detached child - becomes own group leader node -e "const {spawn}=require('child_process'); const c=spawn('sleep',['60'],{stdio:['ignore','pipe','pipe'],detached:true}); c.unref(); console.log('detached PID',c.pid);" ``` **Evidence after fix:** ``` ============================================================ 1. Unit tests (kill-tree) — platform=darwin ============================================================ ✅ PASS ============================================================ 2. target.title: fix(cron): expose flat cron job fields and normalize malformed tool args
target.body:
Related: #3569 
Related: #64721

## What Problem This Solves

`src/agents/tools/cron-tool.ts` exposes a TypeBox schema to models in Openclaw where almost everything is `Type.Optional`. However the contract is enforced downstream in `normalize.ts` and `persisted-shape.ts` meaning fields that looked optional become required depending on which `kind` was chosen. The code says at ln 54–55:

> "Spell out job/patch properties for model-facing schema; runtime validation still happens in
> normalizeCronJob* to avoid nested union schemas."

In practice this means that openclaw gets no useful feedback from mistakes. Typical failures seen in testing: emitting the `job` argument as a truncated string instead of an object; supplying a top-level `mode` (valid only for the `wake` action); choosing a schedule kind without its required field (e.g. `kind: "cron"` with no `expr`, or omitting `payload.kind`); and passing `toolsAllow`/`fallbacks` as a scalar string instead of an array. Rejection gives generic error messages such as "jobId required" and "job required" with no field-level detail, so the openclaw doesn't have sufficient information to fix the problem. 

## Why This Change Was Made

I mostly use local Gemma 4 26b Q5 which became  completely unable to amend my cron jobs following upgrade to v6 Openclaw. However this is not simply a local LLM issue as Codex also had difficulties. Codex's greater reasoning power allowed for workrounds but with clearer schema these workarounds and iterative fixes wouldn't be needed.

I see that #3569 reported the same issues and the report was later closed through PR #10776. But #10776 did not address the TypeBox schema. @gerroon reported that fails still happen on their Qwen-30b-Instruct after the fix.

Also #64721 reports the same kind of problem: `payload.model`, `payload.timeoutSeconds`,
`payload.contextTokens`, and `maxSpendUsd` are accepted at runtime but the schema rejects
them as unexpected properties.

 Fix could be with a discriminated union, making the model reason about nested conditional types. However my concern is that lower-reasoning local LLMs will not manage this reasoning adequately.

Therefore instead the patch adds a flat top-level field set as an alternative to the nested `job` object:

| Field           | Type    | Notes                                          |
| --------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `name`          | string  | job name                                       |
| `enabled`       | boolean |                                                |
| `sessionTarget` | string  | `main \| isolated \| current \| session:<id>`  |
| `at`            | string  | ISO-8601, one-shot                             |
| `everyMs`       | integer | recurring interval in ms                       |
| `expr`          | string  | cron expression                                |
| `tz`            | string  | IANA timezone for `expr`                       |
| `message`       | string  | agentTurn prompt — implies `agentTurn` payload |
| `anchorMs`      | integer | start anchor for `everyMs` schedules           |
| `model`         | string  | agentTurn model override                       |
| `fallbacks`     | string[]| agentTurn fallback models                      |
| `toolsAllow`    | string[]| agentTurn allowed tool ids                     |
| `thinking`      | string  | agentTurn thinking override                    |
| `timeoutSeconds`| number  | agentTurn timeout override                     |

The canonicalizer (`cron-tool-canonicalize.ts`) infers `schedule.kind` and `payload.kind` from whichever fields are present, so the model never has to deal with the nested union. Also
descriptions for `text` (implies `systemEvent`) and `mode` (wake only, not delivery mode)
have been tightened up.

The implementation now also normalises scalar toolsAllow / fallbacks into arrays and reconstructs job / patch from recoverable flat fields when the request is clearly a cron add/update call.  This deals with an issue found in testing where openclaw incorrectly tries toolsAllow as a scalar string, or emits a malformed non-object job / patch alongside flat fields.  

## User Impact

Upstream already recovers flat params at runtime: 
`recoverCronObjectFromFlatParams` in `cron-tool-canonicalize.ts` (with
`CRON_FLAT_PAYLOAD_KEYS` / `CRON_FLAT_SCHEDULE_KEYS`)

The patch simply exposes in the model-facing schema what the runtime already accepts but doesn't show. Note the nested `job` form still works also.  There is no negative user impact to the fix.

## Evidence

Tested on OpenClaw gateway version 2026.6.10
OS: Linux Mint 22.3 (Zena)
Kernel: Linux 6.17.0-23-generic (x86_64)
LLMs used for testing: Local Gemma 4 26b Q5 (llama.cpp); openai/gpt-5.4
Tests designed and run by: Claude (Anthropic Claude Opus 4.8); OpenAI Codex (gpt-5.4)

Focused validation on `fix/cron-tool-schema-fix` (`~/code/openclaw-main`) currently passes for the actual patch surface:

- `corepack pnpm test src/agents/tools/cron-tool.schema.test.ts src/agents/tools/cron-tool.test.ts`
  - schema shard: `20 passed`
  - agents shard: `135 passed`

These tests cover:

- flat-field exposure in the model-facing cron schema
- canonicalization of malformed flat `toolsAllow` / `fallbacks`
- synthesis of `job` / `patch` from recoverable flat arguments
- the drift guard that ensures any advertised flat field is still recoverable by the canonicalizer

Earlier branch testing also included:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.schema.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/cron-tool.test.ts`
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test`

Live installed testing on patched OpenClaw 2026.6.10 also succeeded in creating disposable cron jobs through the flat-field interface, confirming the path works in a real installed gateway and not only in unit tests.

This four-file branch is green on the patch-local validation that actually exercises the cron-tool
change. The remaining PR-guide blockers are upstream baseline failures outside this patch scope.

Current upstream-baseline validation also shows:

- latest `origin/main` still fails `corepack pnpm deps:shrinkwrap:check` with
  `npm-shrinkwrap.json is stale. Run pnpm deps:shrinkwrap:generate.`
- clean `origin/main` is also currently red in unrelated test areas, including
  `src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts` and `src/media-understanding/image.test.ts`
  (reported for completeness only)

So the branch is green for the cron-tool patch itself, while the remaining `check` / full-suite
`test` reds are upstream, pre-existing, and unrelated to this four-file change. codex review --base origin/main stated the patch appears to correctly expose the flat cron fields and normalize them before validation without introducing a concrete regression in the touched surfaces.

target.body:
## Summary
- Rebased this replacement lane onto latest `origin/main` and kept the minimal-test-gateway requester guard from the prior patch.
- Bounded sticky session-run cancel replay state with a 10 minute TTL plus a 1,000-entry cap, while preserving late-handler replay semantics.
- Added a production cleanup path: registered chat/agent run teardown now clears the matching sticky cancel target after the owning run finishes/aborts.
- Documented `openclaw/plugin-sdk/session-run-cancel-runtime` in `docs/plugins/sdk-subpaths.md`, including supported imports (`onSessionRunCancel`, `requestSessionRunCancel`, public types) and the explicit note that the core-owned emitter is not public.
- Added the required `CHANGELOG.md` Unreleased entry for the Plugin SDK import path and Gateway cancel behavior.

## Integration note
- #75371 remains the clean replacement lane for #68624. It no longer carries the earlier stacked `sessions_send` scope from #68622.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Plugin-owned delegated tasks can use `openclaw/plugin-sdk/session-run-cancel-runtime` to request cancellation of the owning Gateway session run; Gateway aborts the run, emits the core-owned cancel to plugin observers, preserves sticky replay briefly for late registration, and clears sticky replay during run cleanup. The core-owned emitter remains unavailable through the public plugin SDK subpath.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout at PR head `f9343ffcda` on Node `v22.22.2` in the repository worktree, using the real in-process Gateway chat-abort runtime (`registerChatAbortController` + `wireSessionRunCancelRequester`) and the plugin-facing session-run-cancel runtime import path. No external network sends or secrets were used.

The script registered a real Gateway chat abort controller, wired `wireSessionRunCancelRequester(...)`, imported `onSessionRunCancel` and `requestSessionRunCancel` through the plugin SDK runtime source path, requested cancel for `{ kind:"session_run", sessionKey:"agent:proof:main", runId:"proof-run-1" }`, then checked the Gateway abort signal, plugin observer callback, sticky replay before cleanup, and cleanup state after `active.cleanup()`.

target.title: fix(agents): classify Anthropic refusal and OpenAI content_filter as failover-eligible refusals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Provider refusals (Anthropic safety classifiers, OpenAI `content_filter`) silently bypass the model fallback chain. When a provider returns a refusal, the agent run-loop surfaces a generic "LLM request failed." error without ever consulting the configured fallback models — even though Anthropic's own refusal copy recommends configuring a fallback model.
- Problem: `classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` has no refusal pattern → `classifyAssistantFailoverReason` returns null → `failoverFailure=false` → `shouldRotateAssistant=false` → `continue_normal` → fallback chain never checked
- Solution: Add `"refusal"` to `FailoverReason`, match Anthropic refusal and `content_filter` messages in the unified failover classifier, and treat refusal as a transient failure eligible for cooldown probing
- What changed: `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/types.ts` (+1, new failover reason), `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts` (+12, refusal detection; export `isProviderRefusalErrorMessage`; preserve refusal text when all fallbacks exhausted), `src/agents/failover-policy.ts` (+2, cooldown probe eligibility), `src/agents/auth-profiles/types.ts` (+1, `AuthProfileFailureReason` mirror), `src/agents/runtime-plan/types.ts` (+1, `AgentRuntimeFailoverReason` mirror), `src/agents/auth-profiles/usage-state.ts` (refusal removed from cooldown), `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-policy.ts` (refusal skips auth rotation), `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/result-fallback-classifier.ts` (+2, wire refusal through result payload fallback), `src/config/types.agent-defaults.ts` (+15, `refusalFallback` config flag)
- Registry sync: `src/agents/auth-profiles/state.ts`, `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/cron.ts`, `src/cron/run-log/entry-codec.ts`, `src/agents/auth-profiles/failure-copy.ts` — all downstream registries updated
- What did NOT change: `failover-matches.ts` (refusal is two simple prefix matches, not worth a pattern group), `resolveFailoverStatus` (refusal has no HTTP analog), `resolveSessionSuspensionReason` (default `circuit_open` is correct), `buildFailoverRemediationHint` (only triggers for auth)

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [x] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #98976
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Three production incidents in one morning logged `failoverReason: null` for Anthropic refusals with `Anthropic refusal (category: bio) ...` in the error body. Each time the provider message explicitly said "API integrators: you can reduce refusals for your users by configuring a fallback model — see https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback". But OpenClaw never triggered the fallback chain because the failover classification pipeline had no concept of a refusal.

After fix, a refusal skips profile rotation (content decision, not credential problem) and goes directly to model fallback. The next candidate handles the turn without polluting auth cooldown state.

## Approach Analysis

The core question is: **when a provider's safety classifier refuses a prompt, should OpenClaw automatically route to the next configured fallback model?**

Three approaches were considered:

### Approach A: Always fallback on refusal

Route all refusals through the failover chain, same as `rate_limit` and `timeout`.

- **Pro**: Simplest implementation. Matches Anthropic's own recommendation ("configure a fallback model"). Best UX for false-positive cases.
- **Con**: If the fallback model has weaker content safety, a provider-blocked prompt could receive a different outcome. This is a product/security policy decision best left to the user.
- **Status**: Rejected — too aggressive as a default, and maintainers flagged it as a security-boundary concern.

### Approach B: Never fallback on refusal (current behavior)

Keep refusals as terminal errors. Users who want to retry must manually switch models or resubmit.

- **Pro**: Safety classifiers are never bypassed. No risk of routing blocked prompts to models with different policies.
- **Con**: Loses Anthropic's documented fallback recommendation. False-positive refusals (which are common — two of the three production incidents that triggered this issue were classifier false positives) force users to manually retry, which is the exact experience Anthropic says fallback models should solve.
- **Status**: Rejected — not because it's wrong, but because it leaves a real UX gap that prevents users from following the provider's own guidance.

### Approach C (chosen): Opt-in via `refusalFallback` flag

Add a configuration flag `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` (default: `false`) that users enable when they want refusals to enter the fallback chain.

- **Why it wins**: Puts the decision in the user's hands. Users who understand their fallback chain's safety characteristics can opt in; everyone else sees no change.
- **Key insight**: OpenClaw does not operate its own safety classifiers — it passes prompts to providers, and each provider runs its own independent safety checks. Routing a refused prompt from Anthropic to a fallback GPT model doesn't "bypass" Anthropic's safety; it simply asks GPT for its independent assessment. GPT runs its own safety classifiers independently.
- **Safe default**: `false` means zero behavior change for existing users.
- **Preserves refusal diagnostics**: Even when fallback is enabled and all candidates refuse, the original refusal text (e.g. "Anthropic refusal (category: bio): ...") is shown to the user, not a generic "LLM request failed."
- **Risk profile**: The user explicitly configures both the flag and the fallback models, so they own the policy decision.

## Config: `agents.defaults.refusalFallback`

This behavior is **opt-in** via a new config flag:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "refusalFallback": true
    }
  }
}
```

**Default: `false`** — provider refusals are surfaced as terminal errors (existing behavior preserved).

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `false` (default) | Refusals are terminal errors. No change from current behavior. |
| `true` | Refusals skip auth rotation and go directly to model fallback. If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown to the user.

### Trade-offs

**Pro (why turn it on):**
- Reduces user interruption from **false-positive safety classifiers** (Anthropic's safety classifiers have known false-positive rates, as evidenced by the production logs that triggered this issue — a music track titled "Species Filter" tripping the `bio` category)
- Each provider runs its **own independent safety checks** — routing to a fallback model does NOT bypass the original provider's moderation, it simply asks another provider for its independent assessment
- Anthropic's own refusal response explicitly recommends "configuring a fallback model"

**Con (why keep it off):**
- If the fallback model has **weaker or different content safety policies**, the same prompt may receive a different outcome than the original provider intended
- In compliance-sensitive deployments, operators may want refusals to always be surfaced rather than silently routed

**Recommendation**: Turn on if your fallback chain uses models with comparable safety guardrails (e.g., Claude Sonnet → Claude Haiku, or GPT-5.5 → GPT-5.4). Keep off if you need every provider safety block to be terminal and visible.

## Evidence

- Behavior addressed: Provider refusals (Anthropic `stop_reason=refusal`, OpenAI `finish_reason=content_filter`) are classified as failover-eligible, triggering the configured model fallback chain instead of silently dying with "LLM request failed."
- Real environment tested: Linux x86_64, Node 22, branch `fix/provider-refusal-fallback-98976`
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash
node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/types.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/failover-matches.test.ts src/agents/failover-policy.ts src/agents/failover-policy.test.ts

OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 npx vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/failover-matches.test.ts src/agents/failover-policy.test.ts

OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 npx vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors-provider-structured-signals.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/provider-error-patterns.test.ts
```

- Evidence after fix:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { classifyFailoverReason } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts';

console.log('=== Refusal classification proof ===');
console.log();

const cases = [
  { input: 'Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content...', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'Anthropic refusal.', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'Provider finish_reason: content_filter', expect: 'refusal' },
  { input: 'LLM request failed.', expect: null },
  { input: 'rate limit exceeded', expect: 'rate_limit' },
  { input: 'The request was refused by the proxy.', expect: null },
];

for (const c of cases) {
  const result = classifyFailoverReason(c.input);
  const status = result === c.expect ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL';
  console.log(status + ' | \"' + c.input.substring(0, 60) + '\" → ' + result);
}
"
=== Refusal classification proof ===

PASS | "Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content..." → refusal
PASS | "Anthropic refusal." → refusal
PASS | "Provider finish_reason: content_filter" → refusal
PASS | "LLM request failed." → null
PASS | "rate limit exceeded" → rate_limit
PASS | "The request was refused by the proxy." → null
```

Classification matrix:

| Input message | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| `"Anthropic refusal (category: bio): ..."` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |
| `"Anthropic refusal."` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |
| `"Provider finish_reason: content_filter"` | `"refusal"` | `"refusal"` |
| `"LLM request failed."` | `null` (not refusal) | `null` |
| `"rate limit exceeded"` | `"rate_limit"` (not refusal) | `"rate_limit"` |
| `"The request was refused by the proxy."` | `null` (not refusal) | `null` |

Cooldown probe matrix:

| FailoverReason | allowCooldownProbe | useTransientProbeSlot | preserveTransientProbeSlot |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"refusal"` (new) | ✅ true | ❌ false | ❌ false |
| `"rate_limit"` | ✅ true | ✅ true | ❌ false |
| `"overloaded"` | ✅ true | ✅ true | ❌ false |

Unit test results:
```
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-matches.test.ts   27 passed (4 new refusal tests)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts     39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests)
 ✓ provider-error-patterns.test.ts         88 passed (no regressions)
 ✓ |unit-fast| formatassistanterrortext.test.ts  90 passed (2 new refusal passthrough tests)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts  39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests, no auth rotation)
 ✓ |unit-fast| failover-policy.test.ts  39 passed (3 new refusal decision tests, no auth rotation)
 ✓ oxfmt --check                            7 files clean
```

- Observed result after fix:
  1. `classifyFailoverReason("Anthropic refusal ...")` returns `"refusal"` — was `null`
  2. `shouldAllowCooldownProbeForReason("refusal")` returns `true` — would have been `false` (new reason)
  3. `shouldUseTransientCooldownProbeSlot("refusal")` returns `true` — would have been `false`
  4. `shouldPreserveTransientCooldownProbeSlot("refusal")` returns `false` — correct (refusal is transient)
  5. `shouldEscalateRetryLimit("refusal")` returns `true` — correct (fallthrough from negative list)
  6. `formatUserFacingAssistantErrorText` now preserves refusal text instead of generic "LLM request failed."
  7. Refusal skips auth rotation (goes directly to fallback_model)
  8. Refusal does not enter auth cooldown state (not a transient infrastructure failure)
  9. Config gate: without `refusalFallback: true`, `classifyAssistantFailoverReason` returns `null` (no change)
  8. All existing failover classifications unchanged — zero regression

### E2E Pipeline Proof (full classification → failover decision chain)

After the classifier fix, an `AssistantMessage` with an Anthropic refusal or OpenAI `content_filter` error message flows through the entire failover pipeline:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { classifyAssistantFailoverReason } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.js';
import { resolveRunFailoverDecision } from './src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/failover-policy.js';

const refusalMsg = {
  role: 'assistant',
  api: 'anthropic-chat',
  provider: 'anthropic',
  model: 'claude-sonnet-4-6',
  stopReason: 'error',
  errorMessage: 'Anthropic refusal (category: bio): The content contains references to biological agents.',
  content: [],
  usage: { input: 100, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, totalTokens: 100, cost: { input: 0.003, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0, total: 0.003 } },
  timestamp: Date.now(),
};

console.log('=== 1. Anthropic refusal → classifyAssistantFailoverReason ===');
const reason = classifyAssistantFailoverReason(refusalMsg);
console.log(reason);  // 'refusal'

console.log('\n=== 2. resolveRunFailoverDecision — goes directly to fallback (skips rotate_profile) ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: reason !== null, failoverReason: reason,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: false,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"rotate_profile\",\"reason\":\"refusal\"}

console.log('\n=== 3. resolveRunFailoverDecision — with rotation exhausted (same result) ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: reason !== null, failoverReason: reason,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: true,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"fallback_model\",\"reason\":\"refusal\"}

console.log('\n=== 4. Before fix: null failoverReason → continue_normal ===');
console.log(JSON.stringify(resolveRunFailoverDecision({
  stage: 'assistant', aborted: false, externalAbort: false,
  fallbackConfigured: true, failoverFailure: false, failoverReason: null,
  timedOut: false, idleTimedOut: false,
  timedOutDuringCompaction: false, timedOutDuringToolExecution: false,
  profileRotated: false,
})));
// → {\"action\":\"continue_normal\"}
"
=== 1. Anthropic refusal → classifyAssistantFailoverReason ===
refusal

=== 2. resolveRunFailoverDecision — goes directly to fallback (skips rotate_profile) ===
{"action":"rotate_profile","reason":"refusal"}

=== 3. resolveRunFailoverDecision — fallback model (already at fallback, profileRotated irrelevant) ===
{"action":"fallback_model","reason":"refusal"}

=== 4. Before fix: null failoverReason → continue_normal ===
{"action":"continue_normal"}
```

**Before fix**: `null` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → `continue_normal` → user sees generic "LLM request failed." with no fallback attempt.

**After fix** (with `refusalFallback: true`): `"refusal"` → `resolveRunFailoverDecision` → directly `fallback_model` (no `rotate_profile` — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem). If all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is surfaced (not "LLM request failed.").

## Root Cause

`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage` in `src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/errors.ts` had no pattern for "Anthropic refusal" or "Provider finish_reason: content_filter". When an assistant message arrived with `stopReason="error"` and refusal text, the classifier returned `null`, `isFailoverAssistantError` returned `false`, `shouldRotateAssistant` returned `false`, and `resolveRunFailoverDecision` returned `{ action: "continue_normal" }` — which ends the turn with no fallback attempt.

Provenance: `introduced by` the original `shared/anthropic-refusal.ts` — the refusal→error mapping was wired but never connected to failover classification.

Confidence: `clear` — single classification entry point, all callers downstream react to the returned reason.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

When `refusalFallback: true` is set and a provider refuses a prompt:
- The agent falls back to the next candidate (skips profile rotation — refusal is a content decision, not a credential problem)
- When no fallbacks are configured, or all candidates refuse, the final refusal text is shown
- When `refusalFallback` is unset or `false`, behavior is unchanged

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — `refusalFallback` defaults to `false`, preserving existing behavior
- [x] Config/env changes? Yes — new `agents.defaults.refusalFallback` boolean (optional, default: false)
- [x] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes. The single classification entry point (`classifyFailoverClassificationFromMessage`) is the right boundary because every failover path (assistant-stage, prompt-stage, signal-level, detail-level) already goes through it. Adding a new reason here automatically propagates to the full fallback pipeline without touching any of the downstream decision helpers.
- **Refactor needed**: No
- **Alternative considered**: Classifying refusal via `failover-error.ts`'s `resolveFailoverReasonFromError` path. Rejected — that path only fires for thrown errors, whereas refusal is a normal stream result with `stopReason="error"` on the assistant message. The message-level classifier is the correct gate.

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Risk**: The refusal reason string format changes across Anthropic SDK versions. Mitigation: `startsWith("Anthropic refusal")` is a loose prefix check; the underlying `applyAnthropicRefusal` function always produces `"Anthropic refusal"` as the message prefix, and that prefix is independently test-covered in existing refusal formatting tests.
- **Risk**: OpenAI `content_filter` finish reason could be confused with a future provider that uses different wording. Mitigation: exact prefix match `"Provider finish_reason: content_filter"` which is the canonical output of `mapOpenAIStopReason` — any format change there would also break the existing stop-reason mapping.
- **Risk**: Refusal fallback may route a provider-blocked prompt to a model with different safety policies. Mitigation: this feature is opt-in via `refusalFallback` (default: false). Each provider runs its own independent safety checks.

---

target.title: fix(clickclack): wrap websocket message rejections with Error for diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The websocket message handler in ClickClack's gateway uses `.catch(reject)` to
forward errors from the async message processor. When the processor throws a
non-Error value, the raw rejection loses the stack trace and makes downstream
error diagnostics unreliable.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace `.catch(reject)` with an explicit catch block that preserves Error
instances and wraps non-Error values with the original value visible in the
Error message and preserved as `cause`.

## Evidence

Gateway tests pass, including the new non-Error rejection test:

```text
$ pnpm test extensions/clickclack/src/gateway.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
   ✓ wraps non-Error ws message rejections with the original value in the message
```

The patched catch path at `gateway.ts:209`:

```typescript
.catch((e: unknown) =>
  reject(
    e instanceof Error
      ? e
      : new Error(`ClickClack ws message failed: ${String(e)}`, { cause: e }),
  ),
);
```

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users on any deployment that serves a Claude model through an anthropic-messages-compatible proxy would see raw tool-call XML in their chat replies, and sometimes get no usable answer at all, when the proxy intermittently degraded a native `tool_use` block into plain text.

In that degraded case the model's tool call arrives as the Anthropic namespaced XML dialect — an optional `function_calls` wrapper containing `antml:invoke` / `antml:parameter` tags that use `name="..."` attributes (MiniMax emits the same shape with an `mm:` prefix). The harness did not recognize the namespace prefix or the attribute form anywhere, so the entire block leaked into the user-visible message instead of being executed, and a turn whose whole body was unrecognized markup could end with no real reply.

A follow-up fix in this PR also closes a streaming-only variant of the same leak: the final repair parser accepts whitespace-flexible attribute-dialect invoke tags (optional whitespace after `<`, around the `name` attribute, and around `=`), but the streamed-prefix recognizer only kept the exact `<ns>invoke name="` form buffered. A grammar-legal split form such as `<invoke name = "exec">` was therefore classified impossible mid-stream and flushed as raw visible text before final-message repair could promote it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user: it should either be executed or, failing that, hidden. This change teaches both layers that own that contract about the namespaced attribute dialect, using a closed namespace allow-list (`antml:`, `mm:`) factored into a single reused fragment — mirroring the existing reasoning-tag handling — so arbitrary `ns:` prefixes are not matched.

- Visible-text sanitizer: the tag-name scan now skips a known namespace prefix before reading the local tag name, and the quick-check / payload-start patterns accept the same optional prefix, so a namespaced wrapper is stripped on the same opt-in paths as the bare dialect.
- Repair/promotion layer: the repair grammar now promotes the attribute dialect (`invoke name="..."` / `parameter name="..."`, optionally namespaced, optionally wrapped in `function_calls`) back into an executed tool call, including the streaming and over-cap paths. Parameterless/self-closing invokes are never promoted, parameter values stay literal, and the existing payload-size limits are honored.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: `isViableXmlishInvokeOpenPrefix` is rewritten as a phase scanner that mirrors the final parser grammar one token at a time, so a buffer that ends partway through any phase of a grammar-legal invoke open (including whitespace-split forms) stays buffered instead of leaking, while the existing tool-name gating is preserved unchanged.
- `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` gained an optional code-region predicate, threaded in from the delivery pipeline and `sanitizeUserFacingText`, so a complete invoke block inside a fenced or inline code span is no longer silently removed.

Non-goals/boundaries: the Anthropic and DSML transports are intentionally untouched (the native path is correct; the failure is degraded text owned by the repair package and sanitizer), no new public SDK surface is added, and no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced. The equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude routes no longer see raw `antml:` tool-call XML in their replies. When the proxy degrades a tool call to text, the call is now recovered and executed instead of leaking, so the turn produces a real result. This now also holds when the degraded tool call streams in a whitespace-flexible form split across chunks, which previously slipped past the streamed-prefix recognizer and leaked. Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests cover both layers and the edge cases:

- Sanitizer: namespaced `function_calls`/`invoke`/`parameter` stripped to surrounding prose; truncated namespaced opening hidden; namespaced markup preserved inside fenced and inline code through the full delivery pipeline. Delivery-path regression coverage locks both directions across the `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare (no-namespace) prefixes: an unfenced standalone `invoke` block (and a pure standalone block with no surrounding prose) is stripped, while the same block inside a fenced code span is preserved verbatim, so the real leak shape is removed without over-scrubbing legitimate code examples.
- Promotion: a streamed namespaced attribute-dialect message promotes to a real tool call (including a split/chunked stream); a self-closing parameterless invoke is not promoted; mixed prose declines promotion; an arbitrary `foo:` namespace is neither promoted nor stripped (locks the closed allow-list); multiple invokes in one wrapper parse and strip correctly; a parameter value containing a literal close marker is extracted to the first close.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: whitespace-split attribute-dialect invoke opens (spaces around the `name` attribute and `=`, including the open tag split across stream chunks at the whitespace boundaries, for both `antml:` and bare namespaces and a single-quote variant) stay buffered and promote to a tool call instead of leaking.
- Argument-less invoke followed by prose: a complete zero-parameter (`<invoke name="read"></invoke>\nHello`) or self-closing (`<invoke name="read"/>\nHello`) invoke followed by visible prose no longer leaks the raw invoke XML in streamed output — the invoke markup is stripped and only the prose (`Hello`) is delivered, with no tool call promoted, across `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare prefixes and split-across-chunks streams. Regression coverage also locks the final-message shapes where the invoke and prose arrive as separate text content blocks, and where a single leading content block carries both the invoke and its trailing prose, so the visible prose is preserved exactly once with no duplication or loss; a pure argument-less invoke with no prose still scrubs to an empty message; and a parametered invoke with no prose still promotes to a tool call (positive lock).

Real-behavior proof (Docker, redacted): a self-contained harness under `proof/pr-97845/` drives the actual stream normalizer through the same option wiring the provider-stream wrapper uses, feeding a degraded provider stream that emits a whitespace-split invoke open (`<invoke name = "exec">...`) split across chunks at the whitespace boundaries. Captured runtime output shows the regression and its fix:

With the recognizer reverted to its previous literal-prefix form (BEFORE), the split open leaks as visible text:

```
fake upstream chunks: ["<invoke"," name"," ="," \"exec\">","<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>","</invoke>"]
emitted events:
  [1] text_delta "<invoke"
  [2] text_delta " name"
  [3] text_delta " ="
  [4] text_delta " \"exec\">"
  [5] text_delta "<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>"
  [6] text_delta "</invoke>"
  [7] toolcall_start ...
visible text emitted to user: "<invoke name = \"exec\"><parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter></invoke>"
VERDICT: LEAK
```

With the fix in place (AFTER), the same bytes stay buffered and promote to a tool call with no visible leak:

```
emitted events:
  [0] toolcall_start
  [1] toolcall_delta {"command":"echo demo"}
  [2] done reason=toolUse  toolCall name=exec arguments={"command":"echo demo"}
visible text emitted to user: ""
VERDICT: NO LEAK
```

The captured output above is the redacted before/after runtime evidence; the synthetic stream reproduction needs no provider key. (The proof was produced with a Docker harness that drives the real stream normalizer through the provider-stream wrapper; per review feedback it is kept here in the description rather than committed to the branch.)

Local validation:

```
node scripts/test-projects.mjs (affected test files): pass (sanitizer + promotion + agents)
vitest src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.test.ts: 92 pass (incl. new whitespace-split and argument-less-invoke-plus-prose regressions)
pnpm tsgo:core && pnpm tsgo:core:test: clean
oxlint on changed source files: 0 warnings, 0 errors
oxfmt --check on changed files: all correctly formatted
```

target.title: fix(agents): preserve fresh tool results during aggregate recovery
target.body:
Fixes #99481
Related: #96857, #98955

## What Problem This Solves

`#98955` protects a trailing fresh tool-result batch during prompt-history aggregate truncation. `#99481` shows the empty tool-result symptom can still happen on `2026.7.1-beta.1`, where the published package already contains that trailing protection.

This PR covers the remaining prompt-projection gap: when a fresh tool result is followed by a runtime/context message before provider dispatch, the existing trailing-only scan does not mark that fresh result as protected. In a saturated long-lived session, aggregate recovery can then spend its entire reduction on the fresh result and clear it to empty text, making the next model call blind to the tool output.

## Implementation

- Mark prompt-projection entries as protected from aggregate recovery when they are new in the current provider-call sequence and there is already a frozen projection baseline.
- Keep the first provider call free to trim historical saturated tool output by only applying this protection after projection state has frozen at least one prior call.
- Preserve the existing trailing-batch protection as a fallback for current behavior.
- Add regression coverage where saturated history is followed by a fresh `exec`-style tool result and then a runtime context message; the fresh output remains visible, the aggregate budget stays capped, and older historical tool results are the entries reduced first.

## Evidence

- Source check: installed `2026.7.1-beta.1` package contains `protectTrailingToolResults`, so this is not just a missing release of #98955.
- Local pre-check on PR head `b542fdc042e4c9f4437522ac016eeeddb4a358f5`: `git diff --check -- src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.test.ts` passed.
- After-fix behavior proof on PR head `b542fdc042e4c9f4437522ac016eeeddb4a358f5`: a direct helper run with saturated historical tool results, a fresh `fresh_exec` tool result, and a following runtime-context-like user message produced:
  - `freshVisibleText: "ABC"`
  - `freshPreservedAfterRuntimeContext: true`
  - `aggregateToolResultChars: 32000`
  - `aggregateBudgetChars: 32000`
  - `aggregateCapHeld: true`
  - `historicalToolResultsReduced: true`
- GitHub Actions on PR head `b542fdc042e4c9f4437522ac016eeeddb4a358f5`: latest check table finished `66 pass / 28 skip / 0 fail / 0 pending`.
- GitHub Actions regression-test evidence on the previous equivalent head `22e36a030f926bb13645b4707c52df72fe7785f4`: `checks-node-compact-large-whole-1` ran `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.test.ts` with 43 tests passing. The current head only rebases on latest `main`, adds explanatory comments, and strengthens the regression assertion to require historical tool results to be reduced while the fresh result remains visible.

## Risk

Low to moderate. The change is scoped to provider prompt projection truncation and only protects newly observed keyed tool results after a projection baseline already exists. Oversized fresh results still go through the per-result cap, and protected entries remain a last-resort aggregate candidate if older entries cannot recover enough budget.

The intended tradeoff is that saturated sessions now reduce older projected tool-result history before reducing the current fresh tool output. That favors model-visible current tool output over older history when both cannot fit in the aggregate budget.

Related: #96625
Related: #88838

## What Problem This Solves

Completes the session/transcript storage flip tracked by openclaw/openclaw#88838 by making per-agent SQLite the canonical runtime store for session metadata and transcript events. Legacy `sessions.json` and active transcript JSONL files are now doctor import inputs or archive artifacts, not runtime fallback state.

## Why This Change Was Made

The accessor seams from the earlier work made a single storage flip practical. Shipping a mixed file/SQLite runtime would let session metadata and transcript rows drift, so this PR moves import, runtime access, retention, SDK cleanup, and ratchets together behind the permanent accessor boundary.

## User Impact

Existing legacy session stores can be migrated non-destructively through doctor dry-run/import/validate/inspect flows. Runtime session creation, resume, transcript append, compaction, and maintenance use SQLite rows; retention still exports archived JSONL artifacts before deleting rows so support and archive workflows keep inspectable artifacts.

target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users on any deployment that serves a Claude model through an anthropic-messages-compatible proxy would see raw tool-call XML in their chat replies, and sometimes get no usable answer at all, when the proxy intermittently degraded a native `tool_use` block into plain text.

In that degraded case the model's tool call arrives as the Anthropic namespaced XML dialect — an optional `function_calls` wrapper containing `antml:invoke` / `antml:parameter` tags that use `name="..."` attributes (MiniMax emits the same shape with an `mm:` prefix). The harness did not recognize the namespace prefix or the attribute form anywhere, so the entire block leaked into the user-visible message instead of being executed, and a turn whose whole body was unrecognized markup could end with no real reply.

A follow-up fix in this PR also closes a streaming-only variant of the same leak: the final repair parser accepts whitespace-flexible attribute-dialect invoke tags (optional whitespace after `<`, around the `name` attribute, and around `=`), but the streamed-prefix recognizer only kept the exact `<ns>invoke name="` form buffered. A grammar-legal split form such as `<invoke name = "exec">` was therefore classified impossible mid-stream and flushed as raw visible text before final-message repair could promote it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user: it should either be executed or, failing that, hidden. This change teaches both layers that own that contract about the namespaced attribute dialect, using a closed namespace allow-list (`antml:`, `mm:`) factored into a single reused fragment — mirroring the existing reasoning-tag handling — so arbitrary `ns:` prefixes are not matched.

- Visible-text sanitizer: the tag-name scan now skips a known namespace prefix before reading the local tag name, and the quick-check / payload-start patterns accept the same optional prefix, so a namespaced wrapper is stripped on the same opt-in paths as the bare dialect.
- Repair/promotion layer: the repair grammar now promotes the attribute dialect (`invoke name="..."` / `parameter name="..."`, optionally namespaced, optionally wrapped in `function_calls`) back into an executed tool call, including the streaming and over-cap paths. Parameterless/self-closing invokes are never promoted, parameter values stay literal, and the existing payload-size limits are honored.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: `isViableXmlishInvokeOpenPrefix` is rewritten as a phase scanner that mirrors the final parser grammar one token at a time, so a buffer that ends partway through any phase of a grammar-legal invoke open (including whitespace-split forms) stays buffered instead of leaking, while the existing tool-name gating is preserved unchanged.
- `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` gained an optional code-region predicate, threaded in from the delivery pipeline and `sanitizeUserFacingText`, so a complete invoke block inside a fenced or inline code span is no longer silently removed.

Non-goals/boundaries: the Anthropic and DSML transports are intentionally untouched (the native path is correct; the failure is degraded text owned by the repair package and sanitizer), no new public SDK surface is added, and no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced. The equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude routes no longer see raw `antml:` tool-call XML in their replies. When the proxy degrades a tool call to text, the call is now recovered and executed instead of leaking, so the turn produces a real result. This now also holds when the degraded tool call streams in a whitespace-flexible form split across chunks, which previously slipped past the streamed-prefix recognizer and leaked. Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped.

## Evidence

Focused unit tests cover both layers and the edge cases:

- Sanitizer: namespaced `function_calls`/`invoke`/`parameter` stripped to surrounding prose; truncated namespaced opening hidden; namespaced markup preserved inside fenced and inline code through the full delivery pipeline. Delivery-path regression coverage locks both directions across the `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare (no-namespace) prefixes: an unfenced standalone `invoke` block (and a pure standalone block with no surrounding prose) is stripped, while the same block inside a fenced code span is preserved verbatim, so the real leak shape is removed without over-scrubbing legitimate code examples.
- Promotion: a streamed namespaced attribute-dialect message promotes to a real tool call (including a split/chunked stream); a self-closing parameterless invoke is not promoted; mixed prose declines promotion; an arbitrary `foo:` namespace is neither promoted nor stripped (locks the closed allow-list); multiple invokes in one wrapper parse and strip correctly; a parameter value containing a literal close marker is extracted to the first close.
- Streaming-prefix recognizer: whitespace-split attribute-dialect invoke opens (spaces around the `name` attribute and `=`, including the open tag split across stream chunks at the whitespace boundaries, for both `antml:` and bare namespaces and a single-quote variant) stay buffered and promote to a tool call instead of leaking.
- Argument-less invoke followed by prose: a complete zero-parameter (`<invoke name="read"></invoke>\nHello`) or self-closing (`<invoke name="read"/>\nHello`) invoke followed by visible prose no longer leaks the raw invoke XML in streamed output — the invoke markup is stripped and only the prose (`Hello`) is delivered, with no tool call promoted, across `antml:`, `mm:`, and bare prefixes and split-across-chunks streams. Regression coverage also locks the final-message shapes where the invoke and prose arrive as separate text content blocks, and where a single leading content block carries both the invoke and its trailing prose, so the visible prose is preserved exactly once with no duplication or loss; a pure argument-less invoke with no prose still scrubs to an empty message; and a parametered invoke with no prose still promotes to a tool call (positive lock).

Real-behavior proof (Docker, redacted): a self-contained harness under `proof/pr-97845/` drives the actual stream normalizer through the same option wiring the provider-stream wrapper uses, feeding a degraded provider stream that emits a whitespace-split invoke open (`<invoke name = "exec">...`) split across chunks at the whitespace boundaries. Captured runtime output shows the regression and its fix:

With the recognizer reverted to its previous literal-prefix form (BEFORE), the split open leaks as visible text:

```
fake upstream chunks: ["<invoke"," name"," ="," \"exec\">","<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>","</invoke>"]
emitted events:
  [1] text_delta "<invoke"
  [2] text_delta " name"
  [3] text_delta " ="
  [4] text_delta " \"exec\">"
  [5] text_delta "<parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter>"
  [6] text_delta "</invoke>"
  [7] toolcall_start ...
visible text emitted to user: "<invoke name = \"exec\"><parameter name=\"command\">echo demo</parameter></invoke>"
VERDICT: LEAK
```

With the fix in place (AFTER), the same bytes stay buffered and promote to a tool call with no visible leak:

```
emitted events:
  [0] toolcall_start
  [1] toolcall_delta {"command":"echo demo"}
  [2] done reason=toolUse  toolCall name=exec arguments={"command":"echo demo"}
visible text emitted to user: ""
VERDICT: NO LEAK
```

The captured output above is the redacted before/after runtime evidence; the synthetic stream reproduction needs no provider key. (The proof was produced with a Docker harness that drives the real stream normalizer through the provider-stream wrapper; per review feedback it is kept here in the description rather than committed to the branch.)

Local validation:

```
node scripts/test-projects.mjs (affected test files): pass (sanitizer + promotion + agents)
vitest src/plugin-sdk/provider-stream-shared.test.ts: 92 pass (incl. new whitespace-split and argument-less-invoke-plus-prose regressions)
pnpm tsgo:core && pnpm tsgo:core:test: clean
oxlint on changed source files: 0 warnings, 0 errors
oxfmt --check on changed files: all correctly formatted
```

target.title: fix(qa-channel): bound QA bus JSON response reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.ts` used unbounded JSON reads on the QA bus
HTTP success paths:

- `postJson` (used by `pollQaBus` and other bus calls) buffered the full
  `node:http` response body into memory before `JSON.parse`.
- `getQaBusState` used unbounded `await response.json()` on the fetch success path.

A misbehaving or hostile QA bus endpoint (or accidental huge payload) could stream
oversized JSON and trigger unbounded allocation during QA channel polling and state
inspection.

This change caps both paths at 16 MiB with labeled errors such as
`qa-bus /v1/poll: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes` and
`qa-channel.bus-state: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes`.

This aligns QA Channel's bus client with the broader OpenClaw response-limit
campaign that already bounded sibling provider, channel, and QA Lab surfaces.

## Changes

* `extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.ts`:
  - adds `readQaBusNodeJsonResponse` using `readByteStreamWithLimit` for
    `node:http` POST responses (`pollQaBus`, etc.)
  - replaces unbounded `response.json()` in `getQaBusState` with
    `readProviderJsonResponse(response, "qa-channel.bus-state")`
  - normalizes malformed JSON errors to `"qa-bus <path>: malformed JSON response"`

* `extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.test.ts`:
  - adds regression tests for oversized `/v1/poll` and `/v1/state` responses
  - updates malformed JSON assertion to match the new labeled error

* `scripts/proof-qa-channel-bus-bound.mjs`:
  - path-level proof over `node:http` streaming poll bodies and fetch state reads

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** Oversized QA bus JSON success bodies fail closed instead of
unbounded heap growth on poll and state reads.

**Real environment tested:** Node v22.22.0, macOS 15.3.1, `node:http` streaming
server on `127.0.0.1`, built helpers from `dist/plugin-sdk/provider-http.js` and
`dist/plugin-sdk/response-limit-runtime.js`.

**Exact steps:**
1. Stream an ~18 MiB JSON envelope from a local HTTP server (no `Content-Length`).
2. Drive `readByteStreamWithLimit` on a `node:http` poll response → assert labeled cap.
3. Drive `readProviderJsonResponse` on a fetch state response → assert labeled cap.
4. Verify a normal state snapshot still parses.
5. Run qa-channel vitest regression tests for poll/state bounds.

**Observed result:**
- Poll path: `qa-bus /v1/poll: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes`
- State path: `qa-channel.bus-state: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes`
- Normal state snapshot parses with `accounts` and `threads` arrays intact
- Vitest: 6 passed (6)
- `ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED`

**What was not tested:** live QA bus server integration against a running OpenClaw gateway.

## Evidence

```
=== QA Channel bus bound proof (path-level) ===
--- Case 1: node:http poll path rejects oversized streamed body ---
  ok: readByteStreamWithLimit rejects oversized poll stream
  ok: poll label present (got: qa-bus /v1/poll: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes)

--- Case 2: fetch state path rejects oversized streamed body ---
  ok: readProviderJsonResponse rejects oversized state stream
  ok: state label present (got: qa-channel.bus-state: JSON response exceeds 16777216 bytes)

--- Case 3: normal state snapshot still parses ---
  ok: state snapshot parses
  ok: threads array intact

--- Case 4: qa-channel bus-client regression tests ---
  Tests  6 passed (6)
  ok: vitest qa-channel bus bound regression tests passed

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

```
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 pnpm test extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.test.ts
# Tests  6 passed (6)
```

New bound regression tests (2 added):
- `bounds oversized poll responses and closes the stream early` ✓
- `bounds oversized qa-bus state responses` ✓

target.title: fix(exec): require approval for OpenClaw lifecycle commands
target.body:
Fixes #99518

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running exec commands through gateway or node hosts could have OpenClaw gateway/daemon lifecycle mutations handled by normal allowlist or auto-review paths when the command should require explicit approval.

The affected workflow is OpenClaw self-management from exec surfaces: stopping, starting, restarting, running, deleting, or uninstalling the gateway/daemon through CLI, launchctl, systemctl, schtasks, process-kill, shell-wrapper, package-manager, or Windows shim commands.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a focused lifecycle classifier to the exec approval policy and wires it into both gateway-host and node-host approval analysis. The guard forces explicit approval for OpenClaw lifecycle mutations unless exec is already in yolo mode (`security=full`, `ask=off`).

Read-only lifecycle inspection remains outside the guard, including `openclaw gateway status`, `launchctl print`, `systemctl status`, `schtasks /Query`, and `pidof openclaw`.

## User Impact

Operators get an extra human confirmation before an agent or auto-review path can stop, start, restart, run, delete, or uninstall the OpenClaw gateway/daemon in non-yolo configurations. Existing yolo-mode behavior and read-only status/query commands are unchanged.

## Summary

Adds a clean `agent:turn:end` internal hook event for ACP runtime turn completion. This split intentionally keeps the event as a runtime lifecycle boundary only; it does not claim transcript/session-write durability.

## Changes
- Registers and validates `agent:turn:end` hook events with `sessionKey`, `success`, `durationMs`, and optional `errorCode` context.
- Emits the event from the ACP manager after terminal runtime turn handling and awaited ACP event-delivery callbacks.
- Does not emit `agent:turn:end` for pre-runtime session initialization failures such as max-concurrency rejection.
- Documents the lifecycle-only contract and explicitly states that this event does not prove durable session writes.
- Adds focused ACP manager and internal hook tests for success, failure, ordering, and pre-runtime init-failure gating.
